answers.answer: The stub is the client's local lookup helper and asks a recursive resolver to obtain the answer. With empty relevant caches the recursive resolver asks root, follows its referral to .example, then that authority's referral to the notes.example authoritative servers. A zone is a managed portion of DNS names; delegation assigns a child zone to its authorities, and a referral points toward those authorities rather than providing the host address. The notes.example authority supplies api.notes.example's CNAME to edge.notes.example. CNAME is a DNS-name alias, not an IP, URL or path; usable target A (IPv4) or AAAA (IPv6) data must be obtained, whether returned with the alias or through another lookup. The resolver returns the result to the stub. Later cached answers or delegations can skip visits, and alias and target records can be cached separately. The client uses a reachable address family, connects, verifies HTTPS for api.notes.example and then sends the HTTP request for /notes/42. DNS resolves api.notes.example, not /notes/42, and does not carry that exchange. An address does not prove Notes is healthy.

evidence.quote: The stub resolver is the client's local lookup helper.
Delegation assigns responsibility for a child zone to its authoritative servers.
An A record supplies an IPv4 address; an AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address.
Alias and target records can be cached separately.
DNS resolves the hostname, not the URL path, and does not carry the later HTTP exchange.
An address answer does not establish that the application is healthy.
The client must still verify the certificate for the hostname it requested

answers.answer: TTL limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds; each cache ages the TTL it received. The 11:59 answer with 3600 seconds can remain ordinarily usable until 12:59, so lowering TTL and changing the address at noon does not require refresh by 12:01. For a safer move, lower TTL first and wait for the previous 3600-second lifetime to age out before switching. Keep the old destination usable through the transition, monitoring traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations; open connections are not migrated. Short TTLs cause more refresh queries and more frequent dependence on working DNS. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent simultaneous cutover, and some resolvers may serve expired data when refresh fails. The lesson supplies no universal exact retirement time: observe clients and connections rather than treating TTL as a hard global deadline.

evidence.quote: TTL, or time to live, limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds.
For a planned move, lower TTL first, allow the previous longer TTL to age out, then switch.
Keep the old destination usable through the transition while monitoring traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations.
Some resolvers can even serve expired data when refreshing fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.

answers.answer: Negative caching temporarily reuses an answer reporting absence. The cached NXDOMAIN means the queried name did not exist; adding the A record does not notify that cache. Its negative lifetime is independent of the new positive record's 30-second TTL, which therefore need not clear it. NXDOMAIN reports absence of the name. NODATA for AAAA says the name exists but lacks the requested AAAA record; it does not show that A is absent or that the name does not exist. SERVFAIL says resolution could not be completed, not that the name is absent. Failures may also be cached to avoid hammering failing servers. Inspect the exact name, requested type and returned status before changing records; the lesson does not give this negative entry's actual expiry.

evidence.quote: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence.
The negative answer has its own cache lifetime; the new positive record's TTL does not clear it.
NODATA means the name exists but has no record of the requested type: no AAAA record does not imply no A record or no name.
SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed
Resolution failures may also be cached to avoid repeatedly hammering failing DNS servers.

answers.answer: Steering selects destinations returned in DNS answers; failover changes the selected destination after failure. A separate health check and policy or an operator must detect east's failure and update answers, since ordinary records do not detect application health. Equal proportions of lookup answers do not imply equal HTTP request counts: a shared recursive resolver can reuse one answer for many clients and each client can send many requests over the selected address or connection. Removing east from new answers leaves cached clients able to try east and does not migrate existing connections to west. DNS does not select anew for every HTTP request. West must be reachable, healthy and have sufficient spare capacity for the redirected work. A sampled health signal and DNS change do not guarantee instant recovery or success of every request.

evidence.quote: DNS traffic steering selects destinations returned in answers. Failover changes the selected destination after failure.
Ordinary DNS records do not detect application health themselves.
A shared recursive resolver can reuse one answer for many clients
Existing connections do not migrate to west just because DNS changed.
West must be reachable, healthy and have enough spare capacity for redirected work.

answers.answer: Clients with usable cached addresses can connect despite a DNS outage, and open sessions may continue on existing connections without a fresh lookup. New uncached users need a reachable recursive resolver, working delegation and answering authorities, so they can fail while those sessions work. Start at the affected client's recursive resolver and inspect queried name/type, answer or error and remaining TTL; compare authoritative records and parent delegation for wrong or failed results. An authoritative new address and cached old address can indicate cache ageing rather than a needed edit. Once the expected address is obtained, investigate connection, HTTPS and application results separately. HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error and is not by itself evidence of a DNS lookup failure. Reachable alternate resolvers and authorities reduce individual DNS server failures but cannot repair shared incorrect records, broken delegation or a failed Notes application.

evidence.quote: During a DNS outage, a client with a usable cached address may still connect, and an open connection may keep working without a lookup.
Start with the client's recursive resolver: inspect the queried name and type, its answer or error, and remaining TTL.
Compare authoritative data and parent delegation when results are wrong or failing.
HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error; it is not by itself a DNS lookup failure.
They cannot fix a shared wrong record, broken delegation or a failed application.

answers.answer: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. The validating resolver checks them through a chain of trust beginning at a configured trusted key, with each trusted signing key vouching for the next link. Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity, so alteration is detectable. It does not encrypt or hide the query, establish Notes health or availability, or replace HTTPS certificate checks. HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client must verify api.notes.example, the requested hostname, even if DNS followed a CNAME to edge.notes.example. Application access rules remain separate.

evidence.quote: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data.
each trusted signing key vouches for the next link, starting at a configured trusted key.
Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity
DNSSEC does not encrypt the query, certify service health or guarantee availability.
HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange.
The client must still verify the certificate for the hostname it requested
